title: The Singh Sabha, 1873
hookLine: Sikhs found reform societies to teach Gurmukhi and renew Sikh practice

lines: IF WE DON'T TEACH IT NOW, IT'S GONE.
A FEW PEOPLE DECIDE TO ACT.
cards: A grandparent's language, and grandchildren who don't speak it anymore. At first nobody notices. The kids answer in English, the recipes stop being written down, the old songs are hummed but not sung.
Then one day somebody realizes: if we don't teach this now, it's gone. Many Sikhs had that feeling in the decades after 1849. The kingdom was gone.
Schools, jobs and prestige ran in other languages. And a handful of people decided to do something. Today: the Singh Sabha.

teach.b: Sabha means an assembly, a society; Singh is the name every Khalsa man carries.
The first Singh Sabha was founded in Amritsar in 1873. It's often said to have been sparked when four Sikh students at a mission school in Amritsar announced they would become Christians.
Many Sikhs felt they were losing touch with their own tradition, and asked why. Their answer was mostly not protest. It was school.

The Singh Sabhas, soon dozens of them across Punjab and beyond, set out to teach Sikhs their own faith. They taught Gurmukhi, the script of the Guru Granth Sahib, so people could read the Gurus' words for themselves.
They printed books, tracts and newspapers in Punjabi, opened schools, and in 1892 helped found Khalsa College in Amritsar. Their scholars wrote histories, dictionaries and commentaries.
One of them, Bhai Kahn Singh of Nabha, spent years helping Max Arthur Macauliffe, an Irish-born official who had left the colonial service, translate the Sikh scriptures into English.
His six-volume work came out in 1909; it's old enough now that anyone may quote it freely, which is why this path names it as its English source. Not everyone in the movement agreed.
Different Singh Sabhas argued, sometimes fiercely, about what Sikh practice should be, and historians still discuss how the movement reshaped Sikh identity.

But its central idea was simple, and it lasted: a community renews itself by teaching its children to read its own words. Many weekend Punjabi classes at gurdwaras around the world today stand in that line.

how: Many gurdwaras run Punjabi and Gurmukhi classes for children, a practice that grew from the Singh Sabha movement's schools; Khalsa College in Amritsar, founded in 1892, is one of its best-known legacies.

games.q: it's the 1870s. your community has lost its kingdom, and many young people are drifting from their tradition. what do you start?
games.why: the Singh Sabhas taught, printed and built schools. renewal began at school.

practice: Here's one letter. The Gurmukhi alphabet is sometimes called the painti, the thirty-five, for its thirty-five letters, and its first letter is ura: say it once, OO-raa; it carries vowel sounds, like the oo in Guru.
If the screen shows it, look at its shape for a few breaths and trace it in the air with a finger, and you'll know the first letter of the script the Guru Granth Sahib is written in.
